passage: Hafsa's cousin Nitin sent her a row of tiny yellow faces at 9 pm: 🙂🙂. Hafsa, eleven, stared at the screen from her bed in the Pune flat. Was he happy? Last week he used the same face when he lost at carrom and said "it's fine." She typed, "Are you ok?" Nitin replied with a crying face and then a heart, then, "Ha ha, I'm ok, just sleepy 😴." Hafsa laughed. "You use that smile for everything!" she wrote. Nitin sent a sticker of a dancing potato. Hafsa still wasn't sure which feeling the smiles meant, so she called him the next morning to hear his voice.

qa.q: What time did Nitin send the row of yellow faces?
qa.a: He sent them at 9 pm.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa ask "Are you ok?" after the smiling faces, and what might the faces really have meant?
qa.a: She remembered Nitin using the same face when he lost at carrom and said "it's fine", so she wondered if it hid a sad feeling. The faces might just have meant he was sleepy, as he said.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do when an emoji is unclear to her?
qa.a: She can ask, as she did, or call the person to hear their voice, rather than deciding what the emoji means on her own.

qa.q: How might Nitin see his smiling faces compared with how Hafsa read them?
qa.a: For Nitin the smile may be a simple all-purpose friendly sign. Hafsa read it as something with a possible hidden mood, so the same emoji meant different things to each.

grounding: A child uses smiling, crying and heart emoji and stickers for mood, and the same emoji is read differently by another person.

passage:
"Why did you send me a crying face, Zubin?" Ritu asked, holding up the tablet at dinner.
"Because I was sad. My tower fell."
"But it was the laughing-crying one. I thought you were laughing."
"It was crying and laughing. Both."
"Then how do I know?"
Zubin thought about it. "Maybe I'll write 'sad' next to it."
"Or send me the heart," said Ritu. "The heart means you love me."
"Bhaiya sent a heart to his teacher yesterday," said Zubin. "Does that mean he loves her?" Ritu burst out laughing. "Ask Papa!" 😄

qa.q: What happened to Zubin's tower?
qa.a: Zubin's tower fell.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he sent the crying face, and why did Ritu read it differently?
qa.a: Zubin felt sad and a bit amused that the tower fell, so Zubin meant both feelings. Ritu saw a laughing-crying face and thought Zubin was laughing.

qa.q: What could Zubin add so that Ritu understands the emoji better?
qa.a: Zubin could write a word like 'sad' next to the emoji, or say his feeling aloud, so the message does not depend on Ritu guessing.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel about needing to guess what the emoji means?
qa.a: Ritu feels confused and a little left out of Zubin's feelings, because Ritu cannot tell whether to comfort Zubin or laugh along.

grounding: A child sends emoji to convey mood, but the same emoji can be ambiguous to the receiver.

passage:
Last summer my friend Elizabeth messaged that she couldn't come to my birthday because her family was going to her aunt's. I stared at the phone for a long time. Then I sent just one thing: 🙂
I meant, "Okay, I'm sad, but I'm trying to be fine." That smile felt heavy to type.
Elizabeth replied, "Yay, glad you're okay!! 😊"
I felt worse. She thought I didn't care at all.
The next day at school I told her the smile was a sad smile. Her eyes went big. "It looked happy to me! My mum sends that one when she's pleased."
Now we have a rule: if it's a sad smile, we add words. She even sent me a voice message singing on my birthday.
- Seema

qa.q: What did Elizabeth reply after Seema's smile?
qa.a: "Yay, glad you're okay!! 😊"

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when typing the smile, and why did it go wrong?
qa.a: Seema felt disappointed but was trying to act fine, so the smile carried sadness; Elizabeth read the same face as pleased, because that is what it means when her mum uses it.

qa.q: What small step did the two friends choose to avoid this mix-up?
qa.a: They agreed to add words when a smile is a sad one, so the emoji is not left to carry the whole feeling.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth probably feel when she learned what the smile meant?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a little sorry, since she had cheerfully replied to what was really a sad message.

grounding: The narrator uses an emoji to show a mood, and a friend reads the same emoji differently, showing how emojis can be ambiguous.

passage:
Class note, Thursday, Class 6 project group
During the science project chat on the school tablets, Chinmay posted a long idea for the volcano model with three diagrams. Trisha replied with a single 👍.
A few minutes later Chinmay came to my desk looking deflated. "She doesn't like it. She just put a thumb."
I asked Trisha, without naming Chinmay. She looked puzzled. "The thumb means it's great! I was typing on the bus and had no time."
I brought them together. Chinmay said a thumb alone felt cold, like "okay, whatever." Trisha said at home everyone uses it for "yes, love it."
Next lesson I asked the whole class what the thumbs-up, the smiley and the heart mean to them. The answers were all different.
- Mr Fernandes

qa.q: How did Trisha reply to Chinmay's volcano idea?
qa.a: With a single 👍.

qa.q: What does Chinmay's deflated look suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Chinmay felt hurt and discouraged, reading the lone thumbs-up as cold, as if Trisha did not like his work.

qa.q: What did Mr Fernandes do next, and why was it a good step?
qa.a: He brought the two together to explain their meanings and then asked the class what common emojis mean to each of them, showing that the same emoji can mean different things.

qa.q: How did Trisha see her own thumbs-up?
qa.a: To Trisha it was warm and positive, the way her family uses it, so she was surprised it came across as cold.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child using an emoji as a feeling and a classmate reading it very differently.

passage:
Sunday
Usha Khala sent a video of her cat trying to jump onto the fridge and falling into the laundry basket. I laughed so hard my stomach hurt. I sent back 😭 because that's what everyone in my class sends when something is SO funny.
Ten minutes later Khala called Ammi. "Is Asif all right? He sent crying faces!"
Ammi handed me the phone and I had to explain that crying faces can mean laughing-crying. Khala went quiet and then laughed. "In my time crying meant crying!"
Now I feel a bit silly. I will send 😂 to Khala from now on, or just type "hahaha". With my friends the crying face is fine.
- Asif

qa.q: What was Usha Khala's cat trying to do in the video?
qa.a: It was trying to jump onto the fridge and fell into the laundry basket.

qa.q: What was Usha Khala feeling when she called Ammi?
qa.a: Usha Khala felt worried and concerned, thinking Asif was upset because of the crying faces.

qa.q: What choice did Asif make to avoid another mix-up?
qa.a: Asif decided to send a laughing face or type "hahaha" to Khala, while keeping the crying face for friends who read it the same way.

qa.q: How might Ammi have seen the phone call?
qa.a: Ammi may have been surprised at first, then amused to see how one emoji could mean opposite things to Asif and his aunt.

grounding: A child uses crying emojis to show laughter, and an adult reads them as sadness, showing emoji ambiguity across people.

passage: In Jasleen's village near Moga, the family phone lived on the shelf beside the milk can. After school she typed to Darshan Chacha, who worked in the city: "Our buffalo had a calf today 🐄 so cute." Then, remembering he wasn't there to see it, she added "😢". Ten minutes later the phone rang. "Jasleen! What's wrong? Is the calf sick?" Jasleen blinked. "No, Chacha, it's fine. I sent the crying face because you're missing it." Chacha laughed, and she could hear his breath let out. "I thought something bad had happened! Send a heart next time for missing." Jasleen typed "❤️" and showed Dadi, who asked why the buffalo was sending love.

qa.q: Where did the family phone live?
qa.a: On the shelf beside the milk can.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen add the crying face?
qa.a: Jasleen felt a little sad that Chacha was missing the new calf; the crying face meant 'I miss you here', not that anything was wrong.

qa.q: What could Jasleen try next time so the feeling is clear?
qa.a: Add a few words with the emoji, such as 'wish you could see it', or use a heart as Chacha suggested, since one face can mean different things.

qa.q: How did Darshan Chacha read the crying face at first?
qa.a: He read it as bad news, perhaps a sick calf, and was worried enough to call; he was relieved once Jasleen explained.

grounding: It illustrates a child using an emoji to carry a feeling and the same crying face being read very differently by the person who receives it.
